Transport layer routing mechanism \\nThe guiding price of a path is calculated based on the carrier quote. \\nAccording to different characteristics, paths are classified into distance \\nvector master path and link-state branch paths, corresponding to inter- \\nautonomous area links and intra-autonomous area links, respectively. \\nIn this study, we developed the CPI routing mechanism based on the \\nfollowing assumptions: (1) The PI containers flowing in the CPI logistics \\nnetwork are all standard boxes with the same weight, volume, and type, \\n(2) Distance vector links can provide sufficient capacity, while link-state \\npaths have limited capacity, (3) Each link is associated with a carrier \\nquote. Links covering the distance vector master path are charged based \\non transport distance, while links covering the link state branch path are \\ncharged based on the number of PI containers to be transported. (4) The \\ncarrier is only allowed to quote once in a short period and the quote \\nremains unchanged for the duration of the logistics process. \\nThe CPI routing mechanism adopted in the CPI transport layer is \\npresented in Fig. 4. At the beginning, the demand quantity and desti-\\nnation of the PI container should be clarified. Then, the status of each \\npath that connects the current node is checked according to the routing \\ntable. If the path status is healthy, it can be quoted by carriers to \\ngenerate links. Correspondingly, road repairs, road closure and the \\nexhaustion of link capacity would cause the path to be identified as \\nunhealthy, and the overhead of unhealthy paths will be set to an infinite \\nvalue to avoid being selected for routing. The routing table is updated in \\nreal time, showing the optimal next-hop path that reaches the destina -\\ntion with the least overhead for the current node at that time. If the next \\nhop is the destination, the routes, routing distance and total overhead \\ncan be output. Otherwise, the current node will be replaced by the next \\nhop, and the process will be re-executed until the PI container reaches its \\ndestination. \\nThe charging methods are various according to different types of \\npaths. Since the market for master paths is saturated, multiple carriers \\ncan provide transport service for a path and the capacity of the distance \\nvector path is sufficient. Neither carriers nor other logistics participants \\ncan affect the market price of links for distance vector paths by \\nmonopolizing the capacity. The market price only depends on the supply \\nand demand. The overhead of a distance vector path mainly depends on \\nthe transport distance. Carriers use unit distance quotes for distance \\nvector paths and compete to provide transport service. Therefore, ac-\\ncording to the DVMP routing mechanism, the unit distance quotes from \\nall participating carriers should first be obtained. Then, the quotes are \\nmultiplied by the distance and the number of PI containers to get the \\ngradient price for the path. The link with the smallest gradient price will \\nbe selected as the optimal link, and the gradient price for the corre -\\nsponding link as the path overhead will be added to the total overhead. \\nThe capacity provided by carriers is generally limited due to the \\nmode of transport in branch paths. They usually give a ladder price \\nbased on the quantity of PI containers. For the reason of limited re-\\nsources, the unit price gets higher as the number of PI containers in-\\ncreases. Therefore, according to the LSBP routing mechanism, the ladder \\nprice quotes from all participating carriers should first be obtained. \\nThen, the guiding prices corresponding to the quantity of PI containers \\nare calculated based on the gradient price. The carrier that provides the \\nlink with the smallest gradient price will be first selected to provide \\ntransport service. However, if too many PI containers are shipped on the \\nsame path, they may be shared by more than one carrier. For instance, a \\ncarrier provides a link with a capacity of 30 units for a unit price of 25, \\nbut from the 31st unit, which is the second link provided by the carrier, \\nthe unit price becomes 30. Another carrier ’s first link provides 20 units \\nof capacity at a unit price of 28, but the unit price for its second link \\nbecomes 32. If a total of 40 units of PI containers are to be shipped to the \\nsame destination, the two carriers will be selected to transport together, \\nand the path overhead should be the sum of the guiding prices of the two \\nlinks. Wu et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      \\nAdvanced Engineering Informatics 60 (2024) 102551\\n147.Conclusion \\nCPI is an emerging paradigm for building global interconnected lo-\\ngistics networks. It constructs a new management paradigm by recon -\\nfiguring the logistics network to improve logistics efficiency. CPI builds \\na cyber layer on top of the PI framework. PI containers are configured \\nand scheduled in cyberspace, enabling seamless flows of PI containers in \\nthe logistics network similar to data packets that are transmitted in the \\ncomputer network. The fusion of the logistics networks is a significant \\nstep to initiate this concept. With an integrated logistics infrastructure, \\ndata and information can be shared and used throughout the logistics \\nnetwork for maintaining stable network operation. \\nAs one of the world’s economic centers, the GBA has complete lo-\\ngistics infrastructures, yet the capability of some logistics infrastructures \\nhas not been effectively developed and utilized. The integration of lo-\\ngistics infrastructure is a key move in promoting the realization of \\nsynergistic development of the logistics industry in the GBA. In this \\nstudy, the two-layered CPI-LI2 framework is proposed to enable the lo-\\ngistics infrastructure integration in the GBA. At the link layer, a LEAF \\nmethod is adopted to divide the region into several autonomous areas \\nand to establish connections between them by electing core autonomous \\nareas and regional link centers. Through the link layer fusion, the lo-\\ngistics infrastructures in the network are integrated. The DVMP routing \\nmechanism and LSBP routing mechanism are proposed based on the \\ndistance vector characteristics and the path state characteristics of the \\npath, respectively. The combination of these two routing mechanisms \\nforms the CPI routing mechanism to coordinate the transport resources. \\nTo validate the CPI-LI2 framework, it is applied to a medical logistics \\nnetwork in GBA. Through a case study, we demonstrate the applicability \\nand extensibility of the framework and the advantages of the CPI routing \\nmechanism in the context of dynamic, large-scale networks. \\nThe CPI-LI2 framework improves interoperability of infrastructure \\nthrough logistics infrastructure integration and enables real-time \\nmonitoring, analysis and decision-making in CPI logistics networks \\nthrough flexible operational mechanisms. The CPI-LI2 framework has \\nthe potential to contribute to the development of CPI in two aspects: \\n(1)This paper proposed the LEAF method to integrate logistics in-\\nfrastructures. This method introduces the concept of computer \\nnetworks and uses clustering methods to divide the logistics \\nnetwork into different autonomous areas, similar to the autono -\\nmous systems in computer networks. In this case, failures in the \\nlocal network do not have a huge impact on the whole network, \\nand the division of areas reduces the size of the database and \\nlowers the requirements for infrastructure capacity. Moreover, the \\nLEAF method improves network response efficiency and disaster \\ntolerance through a weighted distance function and core autono -\\nmous area election. The LEAF method is a combination of several \\ngeneral methods. It considers the influence of realistic factors on \\nthe division of physical network areas and adopts a suitable \\nmethod to construct a reliable physical network link layer, which \\nprovides a solution to the problem of large-scale logistics infra-\\nstructure integration that is influenced by multiple factors.  \\n(2) This paper developed a DVMP routing mechanism for distance \\nvector paths and an LSBP routing mechanism for link state paths \\nat the transport layer and adopted the guiding price as the path \\noverhead, forming a CPI routing mechanism that can flexibly \\nselect the optimal next hop. This mechanism adapts to changes in \\ninfrastructure-integrated logistics networks and ensures efficient \\ndecision-making in large-scale networks. In addition, this mech -\\nanism has portability. Since the guiding price is based on carriers’ \\nquotes, which widely exist in logistics networks for different \\ntypes and different scales, the CPI routing mechanism can be \\napplied in other transportation scenarios (e.g., air transportation \\nand shipping) and even be further developed into a multimodal \\ntransport model. Notably, some specific topics are worthy of further exploration. First, \\nthis study uses the Euclidean distance rather than the actual logistical \\ndistance as the distance between two locations. The main reason is that \\ndistance does not have a large impact on the results, and most studies \\nused the Euclidean distance to design routing mechanisms. If the dis-\\ntance between two locations is given or can be calculated, the Euclidean \\ndistance can be replaced by the actual distance. For another reason, the \\nreality is highly complicated, while the experimental approach in this \\npaper is a simulation based on the principle of simplicity; thus, it is \\nunnecessary to use a complex model consisting of actual paths for \\nresearch. Second, the process of designing the CPI-LI2 framework con-\\nsiders mostly physical factors and neglects human factors. When the \\nregional link centers are elected based on a distance weighting function, \\nthe weights are roughly estimated based on experience. The high levels \\nof standardization and intelligence of CPI infrastructure significantly \\nreduce the manpower required in the logistics process. In addition, labor \\ncosts are only a small part of the operating cost in the logistics process. \\nFinally, there is no comparison between the CPI routing mechanism and \\ntraditional navigation. On the one hand, the CPI routing mechanism \\nproposed in this paper is based on a highly shared intelligent logistics \\nnetwork; however, the current logistics infrastructure and logistics in-\\nformation from different logistics stakeholders are not shared at a high \\nlevel, and there is still a gap compared to an ideal CPI logistics scenario, \\nso this paper cannot force the level of infrastructure sharing. On the \\nother hand, the limited scale of data collected in this paper is not suf-\\nficient to support the comparison of CPI routing mechanisms with \\ntraditional navigation, which is also one of the limitations of this paper. \\nThis part of the work will be supplemented if more comprehensive data \\ncan be obtained subsequently. Although the current research on CPI is at \\nthe stage of theoretical accumulation and validation, the experiments in \\nthis paper can reflect the advancement and feasibility of the CPI concept \\nto some extent. \\nThe CPI-LI2 framework developed in this paper is based on the land \\ntransportation scenario in the GBA. However, one of the characteristics \\nof the logistics network in the GBA is multimodal transport. The current \\nrouting mechanism at the transport layer cannot support multimodal \\ntransport scenarios due to the various data formats and standards in \\ndifferent transport modes. On-time delivery of goods is essential for both \\nfactories and wholesalers, and choosing the shortest distance and fastest \\nmode of transportation could shorten the delivery time, satisfy buyers’ \\nneeds, and increase customer satisfaction. At the same time, wholesalers can also benefit from lower \\ntransportation costs, resulting in more competitive pricing.
